docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Add the following dependency to your project:

MavenGradle

The convenience mcp module bundles mcp-core with Jackson 3.x JSON serialization:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp</artifactId>
</dependency>

This includes default STDIO, SSE, and Streamable HTTP transport implementations without requiring external web frameworks.

If you need only the core module without a JSON implementation (e.g., to bring your own):

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

For Jackson 2.x instead of Jackson 3.x:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp-json-jackson2</artifactId>
</dependency>

If you're using Spring Framework, the Spring-specific transport implementations are now part of Spring AI 2.0+ (group org.springframework.ai):

<!-- Optional: Spring WebFlux-based SSE and Streamable HTTP client and server transport (Spring AI 2.0+) -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp-spring-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- Optional: Spring WebMVC-based SSE and Streamable HTTP server transport (Spring AI 2.0+) -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp-spring-webmvc</artifactId>
</dependency>

Note

When using the spring-ai-bom or Spring AI starter dependencies (spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webflux, spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc, spring-ai-starter-mcp-client-webflux) no explicit version is needed — the BOM manages it automatically.

The convenience mcp module bundles mcp-core with Jackson 3.x JSON serialization:

dependencies {
    implementation "io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp"
}

This includes default STDIO, SSE, and Streamable HTTP transport implementations without requiring external web frameworks.

If you need only the core module without a JSON implementation (e.g., to bring your own):

dependencies {
    implementation "io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-core"
}

For Jackson 2.x instead of Jackson 3.x:

dependencies {
    implementation "io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-core"
    implementation "io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-json-jackson2"
}

If you're using Spring Framework, the Spring-specific transport implementations are now part of Spring AI 2.0+ (group org.springframework.ai):

// Optional: Spring WebFlux-based SSE and Streamable HTTP client and server transport (Spring AI 2.0+)
dependencies {
    implementation "org.springframework.ai:mcp-spring-webflux"
}

// Optional: Spring WebMVC-based SSE and Streamable HTTP server transport (Spring AI 2.0+)
dependencies {
    implementation "org.springframework.ai:mcp-spring-webmvc"
}

docs.title: Bill of Materials (BOM)
docs.text:
The Bill of Materials (BOM) declares the recommended versions of all the dependencies used by a given release. Using the BOM from your application's build script avoids the need for you to specify and maintain the dependency versions yourself. Instead, the version of the BOM you're using determines the utilized dependency versions. It also ensures that you're using supported and tested versions of the dependencies by default, unless you choose to override them.

Add the BOM to your project:

MavenGradle 
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk</groupId>
            <artifactId>mcp-bom</artifactId>
            <version>2.1.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

dependencies {
    implementation platform("io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-bom:2.1.0")
    //...
}

Gradle users can also leverage Gradle (5.0+) native support for declaring dependency constraints using a Maven BOM. This is implemented by adding a 'platform' dependency handler method to the dependencies section of your Gradle build script. As shown in the snippet above this can then be followed by version-less declarations of the dependencies.

Replace the version number with the latest version from Maven Central.

docs.title: Available Dependencies
docs.text:
The following dependencies are available and managed by the BOM:

  • Core Dependencies
    • io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-core - Core MCP library providing the base functionality, APIs, and default transport implementations (STDIO, SSE, Streamable HTTP). JSON binding is abstracted for pluggability.
    • io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp - Convenience bundle that combines mcp-core with mcp-json-jackson3 for out-of-the-box usage.
  • JSON Serialization
    • io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-json-jackson3 - Jackson 3.x JSON serialization implementation (included in mcp bundle).
    • io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-json-jackson2 - Jackson 2.x JSON serialization implementation for projects that require Jackson 2.x compatibility.
  • Optional Spring Transport Dependencies (part of Spring AI 2.0+, group org.springframework.ai)
    • org.springframework.ai:mcp-spring-webflux - WebFlux-based SSE and Streamable HTTP transport implementation for reactive applications.
    • org.springframework.ai:mcp-spring-webmvc - WebMVC-based SSE and Streamable HTTP transport implementation for servlet-based applications.
  • Testing Dependencies
    • io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-test - Testing utilities and support for MCP-based applications.

docs.title: MCP Server (2026-07-28)
docs.text:
Preview

The modern server is a preview in 2.2.0. Its API, in the io.modelcontextprotocol.modern packages, may change in minor releases until 3.0. There is no modern client yet, and some parts of the revision are not implemented. For production servers that talk to today's clients, use the classic server.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The modern server implements the stateless 2026-07-28 MCP specification revision. It lives in io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server, next to the classic server, and shares no types with it: it has its own McpServer, its own McpSchema, and its own transports. Both ship in mcp-core, so no extra dependency is needed.

The 2026-07-28 revision removes sessions and the initialize handshake. Every request carries the protocol version and client capabilities in its _meta, and the server answers each request on its own. The modern server is built around that:

  • No sessions. Any instance can serve any request, so a server scales out without sticky routing.
  • No server-to-client requests. A server that needs input from the user or the model answers with an InputRequiredResult, and the client retries the request with the answers (see Multi Round-Trip Requests).
  • Your catalog, your code. Tools, resources, prompts and completions come from repositories you implement, not from a registry inside the SDK. Per-tenant, filtered, dynamic and paginated catalogs need no extra API.
  • One server, sync or async. There is a single McpServer. You pick sync or async per repository; sync code never sees a Reactor type.
  • Stream only when needed. A handler returns a single result (sent as application/json) or a streaming body that can send progress before the result (sent as an SSE stream).

docs.title: Classic or modern?
docs.text:
Classic server Modern server Package io.modelcontextprotocol.server io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server Spec revision 2025-11-25 and earlier 2026-07-28 Sessions Yes (except the stateless transport) No Primitives Registered specifications Repositories you implement Server-to-client requests Sampling, elicitation, roots, ping Replaced by InputRequiredResult Logging Supported Not supported (deprecated by the revision) Status Stable Preview

By default the modern server only accepts the 2026-07-28 protocol version; change the set with supportedVersions(...) on the builder. A request declaring another version gets an Unsupported protocol version error listing the versions the server supports. Clients that start with an initialize handshake are not supported; serve those with the classic server.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
A server with one tool, served over HTTP:

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.McpSchema.CallToolResult;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.McpSchema.Implementation;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.McpSchema.TextContent;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.McpSchema.Tool;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server.McpRequestContext;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server.McpServer;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server.McpSyncResponse;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server.feature.McpSyncTool;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server.feature.McpSyncToolRepository;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server.feature.ToolsFeature;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server.feature.ToolsPage;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.modern.server.transport.HttpServletMcpTransport;

class EchoTools implements McpSyncToolRepository {

    private final McpSyncTool echo = McpSyncTool.of(
            Tool.builder("echo", Map.of(
                    "type", "object",
                    "properties", Map.of("text", Map.of("type", "string")),
                    "required", List.of("text")))
                .description("Echoes the given text")
                .build(),
            (ctx, request) -> McpSyncResponse.result(CallToolResult.builder()
                .addContent(TextContent.builder((String) request.arguments().get("text")).build())
                .build()));

    @Override
    public ToolsPage list(McpRequestContext ctx, String cursor) {
        return ToolsPage.of(List.of(this.echo.definition()));
    }

    @Override
    public McpSyncTool find(McpRequestContext ctx, String name) {
        return "echo".equals(name) ? this.echo : null;
    }

}

McpServer server = McpServer.builder()
    .serverInfo(Implementation.builder("echo-server", "1.0.0").build())
    .feature(ToolsFeature.ofSync(new EchoTools()))
    .build();

HttpServletMcpTransport transport = HttpServletMcpTransport.builder(server)
    .endpoint("/mcp")
    .build();

// Register `transport` as a servlet in your container, mapped to /mcp,
// with async support enabled.

McpServer is immutable and stateless. build() collects the capabilities of the registered features and serves server/discover from them. There is nothing to start; on shutdown, server.closeGracefully() ends open subscriptions/listen streams with a complete result (see Change Notifications).

Builder options:

Method Purpose serverInfo(Implementation) Required. Sent in _meta of every result. instructions(String) Instructions for the model, returned by server/discover. feature(McpFeature) / features(List) Register tools, resources, prompts, completions or a custom feature. subscriptions(McpChangePublisher) Enable subscriptions/listen. See Change Notifications. requestStateCodec(RequestStateCodec) Seal requestState. See Securing requestState. discoverCache(long ttlMs, CacheScope) Caching hints for server/discover. See Caching. supportedVersions(List<String>) Protocol versions to accept. Defaults to 2026-07-28. jsonMapper(McpJsonMapper) JSON mapper. Defaults to McpJsonDefaults.getMapper().

docs.title: Streamable HTTP (Servlet)
docs.text:
HttpServletMcpTransport is a Jakarta Servlet. It accepts POST only, one request or notification per call. Requests are served on the container thread, so thread-locals set by servlet filters (security context, tracing) are visible to sync handlers. subscriptions/listen streams are served asynchronously, so the servlet and all filters in front of it must support async requests.

HttpServletMcpTransport transport = HttpServletMcpTransport.builder(server)
    .endpoint("/mcp")
    .contextExtractor(request -> request.getUserPrincipal() == null ? McpTransportContext.EMPTY
            : McpTransportContext.create(Map.of("user", request.getUserPrincipal().getName())))
    .httpHeaderValidator(DefaultServerTransportSecurityValidator.builder()
        .allowedOrigin("https://app.example.com")
        .allowedHost("mcp.example.com")
        .build())
    .keepAliveInterval(Duration.ofSeconds(15))
    .build();
Method Default Purpose endpoint(String) /mcp The path the transport answers on. contextExtractor(...) empty context Builds the McpTransportContext handlers see. Runs on the container thread before dispatch. httpHeaderValidator(...) rejects any Origin Validates headers before the body is read. See HTTP Security. maxRequestSize(int) 16 MiB Maximum request body size. keepAliveInterval(Duration) 30 seconds SSE comment interval on open streams; also detects clients that went away. null disables it. errorStatus(int code, int status) see below HTTP status for a JSON-RPC error code.

JSON-RPC errors are answered with the HTTP status the specification assigns: 400 for parse errors, invalid requests, invalid params, header mismatches, missing client capabilities and unsupported protocol versions, and 404 for unknown methods. Other codes are answered with 200. Once a stream has started, errors are sent in-band.

Call transport.closeGracefully() on shutdown. It stops accepting requests and also calls server.closeGracefully(), which ends open subscriptions/listen streams with a complete result.

The servlet requires the routing headers the 2026-07-28 HTTP transport defines, and checks them against the request body:

  • Mcp-Method is required on every request and must equal the JSON-RPC method.
  • MCP-Protocol-Version is required when the body declares a protocol version in _meta, and must match it.
  • Mcp-Name is required on tools/call and prompts/get (the name) and resources/read (the uri), and must match it.

A request with a missing or mismatched header is rejected with error -32020 (header mismatch, HTTP 400) before it is dispatched. Filters can therefore route or authorize on these headers without reading the body. Keep this in mind when testing with curl or another hand-written client.

docs.title: STDIO
docs.text:
StdioMcpTransport reads one JSON-RPC message per line from stdin and writes responses to stdout. Requests are handled concurrently, cancellation is supported, and a single writer keeps output lines intact.

StdioMcpTransport transport = new StdioMcpTransport(server, McpJsonDefaults.getMapper());

// Serve until stdin is closed or closeGracefully() is called.
transport.start().block();

The transport's threads are daemon threads, so block on start() to keep the process alive. Messages longer than 16M characters are dropped; use the five-argument constructor to change the limit.

Unlike the Servlet transport, StdioMcpTransport.closeGracefully() does not call server.closeGracefully(): it cancels in-flight requests, including open subscriptions/listen streams, without sending their pending output. If you use change notifications, call server.closeGracefully() before closing the transport.

STDIO has no headers and no contextExtractor: handlers always see a transport context without user entries, so anything that reads identity from transportContext(), such as a requestState principal binding, has nothing to read.

docs.title: HTTP Security
docs.text:
Authentication and authorization belong in servlet filters in front of HttpServletMcpTransport, including 401/403 challenges. To pass the authenticated identity to handlers, read it in the contextExtractor and put it in the McpTransportContext.

Against DNS rebinding, the transport validates headers with a ServerHttpHeaderValidator before reading the body. The default validator has no allowed origins and no allowed hosts, which means:

  • A request without an Origin header (a non-browser client) passes.
  • A request with an Origin header is rejected with 403, whether it is cross-origin or same-origin. A browser application calling the server must have its origin allowed explicitly.
  • The Host header is not checked.

Configure DefaultServerTransportSecurityValidator with allowedOrigin(...) to accept browser clients, and with allowedHost(...) to turn on Host validation, as in the example above. See HTTP Transport Security for the validator options.

docs.title: Features and Repositories
docs.text:
A feature serves a set of JSON-RPC methods and contributes capabilities to server/discover. The SDK provides one feature per primitive, each backed by a repository you implement:

Feature Methods Sync repository Async repository ToolsFeature tools/list, tools/call McpSyncToolRepository McpAsyncToolRepository ResourcesFeature resources/list, resources/templates/list, resources/read McpSyncResourceRepository McpAsyncResourceRepository PromptsFeature prompts/list, prompts/get McpSyncPromptRepository McpAsyncPromptRepository

Create a feature with ofSync(repository) or ofAsync(repository). Register only the features you need; the server advertises a capability only when its feature is registered. completion/complete has no feature of its own: the prompts and resources features answer it for their own references, see Completions.

Every repository method receives the McpRequestContext, so a repository can return a different catalog per tenant or user. Two rules apply to list:

  • The order must be deterministic, and the result must not depend on the connection.
  • An unrecognized cursor must be answered with McpException.invalidParams(...).

To paginate, return a page with a nextCursor, for example new ToolsPage(tools, nextCursor, null, null).

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
A repository lists tool definitions and finds a tool by name. find returns an McpSyncTool, which pairs a Tool definition with its handler, or null if there is no such tool (the client then gets an Unknown tool error).

McpSyncTool weather = McpSyncTool.of(
        Tool.builder("get_weather", jsonMapper, """
                {
                  "type": "object",
                  "properties": { "city": { "type": "string" } },
                  "required": ["city"]
                }
                """)
            .outputSchema(jsonMapper, """
                {
                  "type": "object",
                  "properties": { "temperature": { "type": "number" } },
                  "required": ["temperature"]
                }
                """)
            .build(),
        (ctx, request) -> {
            double temperature = weatherService.temperature((String) request.arguments().get("city"));
            return McpSyncResponse.result(CallToolResult.builder()
                .structuredContent(Map.of("temperature", temperature))
                .build());
        });

The tools feature validates both directions:

  • Input: arguments are validated against inputSchema before the handler runs. Invalid arguments are answered with a CallToolResult with isError: true, so the model can correct the call.
  • Output: when the tool declares an outputSchema, a successful result must carry structuredContent that conforms to it. A missing or invalid structuredContent is a server bug and is answered with an internal error. When a result has structuredContent but no content, the feature adds its JSON as text content.

To use a different JSON mapper, schema validator or cache defaults, use ToolsFeature.ofSync(repository, jsonMapper, jsonSchemaValidator, defaultTtlMs, defaultCacheScope).

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
A resource repository lists resources and, optionally, resource templates, and finds a resource by URI. find returns an McpSyncResource holding the read handler, or null if the URI is unknown. Templates are not matched for you: find receives every URI and decides what it serves.

class FileResources implements McpSyncResourceRepository {

    @Override
    public ResourcesPage list(McpRequestContext ctx, String cursor) {
        return ResourcesPage.of(List.of(
                Resource.builder("file:///config.json", "Configuration")
                    .mimeType("application/json")
                    .build()));
    }

    @Override
    public ResourceTemplatesPage listTemplates(McpRequestContext ctx, String cursor) {
        return ResourceTemplatesPage.of(List.of(
                ResourceTemplate.builder("file:///logs/{date}", "Daily log").build()));
    }

    @Override
    public McpSyncResource find(McpRequestContext ctx, String uri) {
        String content = files.read(uri); // null if the URI is unknown
        if (content == null) {
            return null;
        }
        return McpSyncResource.of((c, request) -> McpSyncResponse.result(ReadResourceResult
            .builder(List.of(TextResourceContents.builder(uri, content).build()))
            .build()));
    }

    @Override
    public boolean supportsSubscribe() {
        return true; // see Change Notifications
    }

}

listTemplates, findTemplate, supportsSubscribe and supportsCompletion have defaults: no templates, no subscriptions and no completion. findTemplate is only needed to complete template variables. Returning true from supportsSubscribe advertises resources.subscribe only when the server also has a change publisher registered with subscriptions(...), because resource updates are only delivered over subscriptions/listen.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text:
A prompt repository lists Prompt definitions and finds an McpSyncPrompt by name, which pairs the definition with a handler returning a GetPromptResult. Required prompt arguments declared in the definition are checked before the handler runs; a missing one is answered with an invalid-params error.

McpSyncPrompt review = McpSyncPrompt.of(
        Prompt.builder("code_review")
            .description("Review a piece of code")
            .arguments(List.of(PromptArgument.builder("code").required(true).build()))
            .build(),
        (ctx, request) -> McpSyncResponse.result(GetPromptResult
            .builder(List.of(PromptMessage
                .builder(Role.USER, TextContent.builder("Please review:\n" + request.arguments().get("code")).build())
                .build()))
            .build()));

docs.title: Completions
docs.text:
Completion suggests values for a prompt argument or a resource template variable. The completion handler belongs to the prompt or template it completes:

McpSyncPrompt review = McpSyncPrompt.of(definition, handler)
    .withCompletionHandler((ctx, request) -> CompleteResult.of(new CompleteResult.Completion(
            languages.stream().filter(l -> l.startsWith(request.argument().value())).toList())));

McpSyncResourceTemplate logs = McpSyncResourceTemplate.of(ResourceTemplate.builder("file:///logs/{date}", "Daily log").build())
    .withCompletionHandler((ctx, request) -> CompleteResult.of(new CompleteResult.Completion(logDates())));

A prompt repository returns such a prompt from find. A resource repository returns such a template from findTemplate(ctx, uriTemplate), which is looked up by the exact uriTemplate string the client sends in a ref/resource reference. Either repository opts in by returning true from supportsCompletion():

class Prompts implements McpSyncPromptRepository {
    // list, find ...

    @Override
    public boolean supportsCompletion() {
        return true;
    }
}

The server then serves completion/complete and advertises completions, sending ref/prompt requests to the prompts feature and ref/resource requests to the resources feature. A custom feature completes its own reference types the same way, by returning them from McpFeature.completionRefTypes() and answering McpFeature.complete(ctx, request). Two features completing the same reference type fail the build.

A reference type no feature completes, an unknown prompt or template, or an argument the prompt or template does not declare, is answered with an invalid-params error. A prompt or template without a completion handler completes to no values. Arguments already filled in by the user arrive in request.context(). At most 100 values are sent; the rest are cut and hasMore is set.

docs.title: Sync and Async
docs.text:
Sync and async repositories can be mixed in one server. A sync repository is adapted to the async API inside the feature; where its code runs depends on the transport:

  • HttpServletMcpTransport resolves requests in blocking mode, so sync code runs on the container thread.
  • Otherwise, sync code runs on Reactor's boundedElastic scheduler.

McpRequestContext.isBlocking() tells you which applies to the current request.

An async repository returns Monos: list returns Mono<ToolsPage>, find returns Mono<McpAsyncTool> (empty if there is no such tool), and handlers return Mono<McpAsyncResponse<...>>.

McpAsyncTool echo = McpAsyncTool.of(echoDefinition,
        (ctx, request) -> Mono.just(McpAsyncResponse.result(CallToolResult.builder()
            .addContent(TextContent.builder((String) request.arguments().get("text")).build())
            .build())));

docs.title: Request Context
docs.text:
Every repository method and handler receives an McpRequestContext, built fresh for each request:

Method Returns method() The JSON-RPC method, e.g. tools/call. requestId() The JSON-RPC request id. protocolVersion() The protocol version from _meta. clientCapabilities() The client capabilities from _meta. clientInfo() The client info from _meta, if sent. For display and logging only. progressToken() The progress token, or null. meta() The raw _meta map. transportContext() The McpTransportContext built by the Servlet transport's contextExtractor. Over STDIO it carries no user entries. isRetry() Whether the request is a multi round-trip retry. isBlocking() Whether sync code runs on the calling thread.

docs.title: Streaming Responses
docs.text:
A handler answers with McpSyncResponse.result(...) for a single JSON response, or with McpSyncResponse.streaming(...) to send notifications before the result. The streaming body runs once the transport has opened the response stream and receives an McpSyncNotifier:

(ctx, request) -> McpSyncResponse.streaming(notifier -> {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
        processChunk(i);
        notifier.progress(i * 10, 100.0, "Processed chunk " + i);
    }
    return CallToolResult.builder()
        .addContent(TextContent.builder("Done").build())
        .build();
})

progress is a no-op when the request carries no progress token, or when the value does not increase. notify(method, params) sends any other request-scoped notification. The async equivalent is McpAsyncResponse.streaming(notifier -> ...) with an McpAsyncNotifier whose methods return Mono<Void>.

Return a streaming response only when you send notifications; a plain result is cheaper for the client and any proxies in between.

docs.title: Required Client Capabilities
docs.text:
A tool, resource or prompt that only works with clients declaring certain capabilities can say so. The server rejects calls from other clients with error -32021 (missing required client capability), listing what is missing, without running the handler:

ClientCapabilities needsSampling = ClientCapabilities.builder().sampling().build();

McpSyncTool summarize = McpSyncTool.of(summarizeDefinition, needsSampling, handler);

McpSyncResource.of(...) and McpSyncPrompt.of(...) take the same optional argument.

docs.title: Multi Round-Trip Requests
docs.text:
The 2026-07-28 revision has no server-to-client requests. Instead, a tools/call, resources/read or prompts/get handler that needs input answers with an InputRequiredResult. It lists the input requests (elicitation, sampling, roots), each under a key you choose. The client fulfils them and retries the original request with the answers in inputResponses, keyed the same way.

(ctx, request) -> {
    Optional<ElicitResponse> answer = InputResponses.get(
            request.inputResponses(), "user_name", ElicitResponse.class, jsonMapper);
    if (answer.isEmpty() || !"accept".equals(answer.get().action())) {
        return McpSyncResponse.result(InputRequiredResult.builder()
            .elicit("user_name", ElicitFormRequest.builder("What is your name?", Map.of(
                    "type", "object",
                    "properties", Map.of("name", Map.of("type", "string")),
                    "required", List.of("name")))
                .build())
            .build());
    }
    return McpSyncResponse.result(CallToolResult.builder()
        .addContent(TextContent.builder("Hello, " + answer.get().content().get("name") + "!").build())
        .build());
}

// Your own type for the shape of an elicitation response
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
record ElicitResponse(String action, Map<String, Object> content) {
}

InputRequiredResult.builder() offers elicit(key, ElicitFormRequest), elicitUrl(key, message, url), createMessage(key, CreateMessageRequest) and listRoots(key). InputResponses.get(...) converts a response to a type of your choice and answers malformed responses with an invalid-params error.

A handler may only request input the client declared it can provide. Requesting anything else is a server bug and is answered with an internal error. Either check ctx.clientCapabilities() before asking, or declare the capability as required so that other clients are rejected up front.

docs.title: Carrying State Across Rounds
docs.text:
A handler that needs to remember something between rounds puts it in requestState(String). The client returns it unchanged with the retry, and the handler reads it from request.requestState():

return McpSyncResponse.result(InputRequiredResult.builder()
    .elicit("step2", ElicitFormRequest.builder("What is your favorite color?", colorSchema).build())
    .requestState("round-2:" + name)
    .build());

docs.title: Securing requestState
docs.text:
The server seals requestState before sending it and opens it on retry, so handlers only ever see state they issued themselves. A tampered, expired or misdirected state is rejected with an invalid-params error before the handler runs.

The default HmacRequestStateCodec signs the state with HMAC-SHA256 and binds it to an expiry (10 minutes by default), to the method and tool, resource or prompt name, and optionally to a principal. Without a configured key it generates a random key per process, and logs a warning. That works for a single instance; with more than one instance, configure a shared key so that any instance can open state sealed by another:

McpServer server = McpServer.builder()
    .serverInfo(serverInfo)
    .feature(ToolsFeature.ofSync(tools))
    .requestStateCodec(HmacRequestStateCodec.builder()
        .key(sharedSecret) // byte[], at least 32 bytes recommended
        .ttl(Duration.ofMinutes(5))
        .principalExtractor(transportContext -> (String) transportContext.get("user"))
        .build())
    .build();

The principal binding only applies when the transport puts an identity in the transport context; over STDIO the extractor above always returns null, so state is not bound to a user.

Sealing bounds the replay window but does not make the state single-use. Where that matters, enforce it in your handler. To use another scheme, implement RequestStateCodec.

Results of retried requests are marked as not cacheable.

docs.title: Change Notifications
docs.text:
Clients learn about catalog changes through subscriptions/listen, a long-lived stream that the server feeds from an McpChangePublisher. McpChangeFeed is a ready-made in-memory publisher; register it with subscriptions(...) and call broadcast(...) when something changes:

McpChangeFeed changes = new McpChangeFeed();

McpServer server = McpServer.builder()
    .serverInfo(serverInfo)
    .feature(ToolsFeature.ofSync(tools))
    .feature(ResourcesFeature.ofSync(resources))
    .subscriptions(changes)
    .build();

// Later, when the catalog changes:
changes.broadcast(new ServerChange.ToolsListChanged());
changes.broadcast(new ServerChange.ResourceUpdated("file:///config.json"));

The change types are ToolsListChanged, PromptsListChanged, ResourcesListChanged and ResourceUpdated(uri). Each is forwarded only if the matching feature is registered; ResourceUpdated also requires the resource repository's supportsSubscribe() to return true. Changes broadcast while no client is listening are dropped.

McpChangeFeed only reaches listeners connected to the same instance. With several instances, implement McpChangePublisher over a shared message bus so that every instance sees every change.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
The 2026-07-28 revision lets list results, resources/read results and server/discover carry caching hints: ttlMs and a cacheScope of PUBLIC or PRIVATE. By default the server sends ttlMs: 0 with PRIVATE, meaning "do not cache".

  • Set defaults for a feature with its full factory, for example PromptsFeature.ofSync(repository, jsonMapper, 60_000, CacheScope.PRIVATE).
  • Override them per page through the ttlMs and cacheScope fields of ToolsPage, ResourcesPage, ResourceTemplatesPage or PromptsPage. Every page of one listing must use the same cacheScope.
  • Set hints for a resource read on the result itself, with ReadResourceResult.builder(...).ttlMs(...) and .cacheScope(...). The feature defaults apply to list results only.
  • Set hints for server/discover with McpServer.builder().discoverCache(ttlMs, cacheScope).

Use PUBLIC only for results that contain nothing user-specific; a shared cache may serve them to any user.

docs.title: Custom Headers (SEP-2243)
docs.text:
A tool can ask clients to mirror selected arguments into HTTP headers, so that gateways and filters can route or authorize on them without parsing the body. Mark the argument in the input schema with x-mcp-header:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "region": { "type": "string", "x-mcp-header": "Region" }
  }
}

A client calling this tool over HTTP sends Mcp-Param-Region with the value of region. The tools feature checks the header against the argument and rejects a mismatch with error -32020 (header mismatch, HTTP 400) before input-schema validation. Annotations that are not valid are logged as a warning and not enforced; compliant clients drop such tools from their listing. Over STDIO there are no headers, and the check is skipped.

docs.title: Custom Features
docs.text:
McpFeature is the extension point the built-in features use, and it is open to you. A feature declares the methods it serves, handles them, and can contribute capabilities and opt methods into multi round-trip requests:

class EchoFeature implements McpFeature {

    @Override
    public Set<String> methods() {
        return Set.of("example/echo");
    }

    @Override
    public Mono<? extends McpAsyncResponse<? extends Result>> handle(McpRequestContext ctx, Object params) {
        // EchoResult is your own type implementing McpSchema.Result
        return Mono.just(McpAsyncResponse.result(new EchoResult(params)));
    }

    @Override
    public void capabilities(ServerCapabilities.Builder builder) {
        // Optional: advertise what this feature adds in server/discover
    }

}

Each method may be served by one feature only; build() fails on duplicates. server/discover and subscriptions/listen are provided by the server. A result must have a non-empty resultType; one without is answered with an internal error.

Methods listed in inputRequiredMethods() may answer with an InputRequiredResult. On retry, the server opens and verifies their requestState before calling the handler, which receives the original, unsealed value. For methods not listed, the server does not touch requestState: a handler that reads it gets whatever the client sent, unverified. List every method that relies on requestState.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• Throw (or, in async code, signal) an McpException to answer with a JSON-RPC error. Its code, message and data are sent to the client as given. McpException.invalidParams(...) covers the common case.
  • Any other exception is treated as a bug: it is logged, and the client gets a generic Internal error, so exception messages that may expose internals stay on the server.
  • For tool failures the model should see and react to, return a CallToolResult with isError(true) instead of throwing. See Error Handling for the distinction between the two tiers.

docs.title: Not Yet Supported
docs.text:
• A modern client. Use the conformance suite or another SDK's client to exercise the server.
  • Tasks.
  • Logging, which the 2026-07-28 revision deprecates. The modern server never sends log messages.
  • Spring WebMVC and WebFlux transports. Spring AI's transports target the classic server.

For a larger working example, see the modern conformance server, which passes all required 2026-07-28 conformance scenarios. It covers the Servlet transport, tools, resources, prompts, completions, streaming, required capabilities, multi round-trip requests and change notifications.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The MCP Server is a foundational component in the Model Context Protocol (MCP) architecture that provides tools, resources, and capabilities to clients. It implements the server-side of the protocol, responsible for:

  • Exposing tools that clients can discover and execute
  • Managing resources with URI-based access patterns and resource templates
  • Providing prompt templates and handling prompt requests
  • Supporting capability negotiation with clients
  • Providing argument autocompletion suggestions (completions)
  • Implementing server-side protocol operations
  • Managing concurrent client connections
  • Providing structured logging and notifications

Tip

The core io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp module provides STDIO, SSE, and Streamable HTTP server transport implementations without requiring external web frameworks.

Spring-specific transport implementations (mcp-spring-webflux, mcp-spring-webmvc) are now part of Spring AI 2.0+ (group org.springframework.ai) and are no longer shipped by this SDK. See the MCP Server Boot Starter documentation for Spring-based server setup.

2026-07-28 specification

This page covers the classic server, which implements the 2025-11-25 specification and earlier revisions. A stateless server for the 2026-07-28 revision is available as a preview; see MCP Server (2026-07-28).

The server supports both synchronous and asynchronous APIs, allowing for flexible integration in different application contexts.

Sync APIAsync API 
// Create a server with custom configuration
McpSyncServer syncServer = McpServer.sync(transportProvider)
    .serverInfo("my-server", "1.0.0")
    .capabilities(ServerCapabilities.builder()
        .resources(false, true)  // Resource support: subscribe=false, listChanged=true
        .tools(true)             // Enable tool support with list changes
        .prompts(true)           // Enable prompt support with list changes
        .completions()           // Enable completions support
        .logging()               // Enable logging support
        .build())
    .build();

// Register tools, resources, and prompts
syncServer.addTool(syncToolSpecification);
syncServer.addResource(syncResourceSpecification);
syncServer.addPrompt(syncPromptSpecification);

// Close the server when done
syncServer.close();

// Create an async server with custom configuration
McpAsyncServer asyncServer = McpServer.async(transportProvider)
    .serverInfo("my-server", "1.0.0")
    .capabilities(ServerCapabilities.builder()
        .resources(false, true)  // Resource support: subscribe=false, listChanged=true
        .tools(true)             // Enable tool support with list changes
        .prompts(true)           // Enable prompt support with list changes
        .completions()           // Enable completions support
        .logging()               // Enable logging support
        .build())
    .build();

// Register tools, resources, and prompts
asyncServer.addTool(asyncToolSpecification)
    .doOnSuccess(v -> logger.info("Tool registered"))
    .subscribe();

asyncServer.addResource(asyncResourceSpecification)
    .doOnSuccess(v -> logger.info("Resource registered"))
    .subscribe();

asyncServer.addPrompt(asyncPromptSpecification)
    .doOnSuccess(v -> logger.info("Prompt registered"))
    .subscribe();

// Close the server when done
asyncServer.close()
    .doOnSuccess(v -> logger.info("Server closed"))
    .subscribe();

docs.title: Server Types
docs.text:
The SDK supports multiple server creation patterns depending on your transport requirements:

// Single-session server with SSE transport provider
McpSyncServer server = McpServer.sync(sseTransportProvider).build();

// Streamable HTTP server
McpSyncServer server = McpServer.sync(streamableTransportProvider).build();

// Stateless server (no session management)
McpSyncServer server = McpServer.sync(statelessTransport).build();

docs.title: Server Transport Providers
docs.text: The transport layer in the MCP SDK is responsible for handling the communication between clients and servers. It provides different implementations to support various communication protocols and patterns. The SDK includes several built-in transport provider implementations:

docs.title: STDIO
docs.text:
Create process-based transport using stdin/stdout:

StdioServerTransportProvider transportProvider =
    new StdioServerTransportProvider(McpJsonDefaults.getMapper());

Provides bidirectional JSON-RPC message handling over standard input/output streams with non-blocking message processing, serialization/deserialization, and graceful shutdown support.

Key features:

  • Bidirectional communication through stdin/stdout
  • Process-based integration support
  • Simple setup and configuration
  • Lightweight implementation

docs.title: Streamable HTTP
SSE HTTP (Legacy)
HTTP Transport Security
docs.text:
Warning

HTTP transports do not validate the Origin or Host headers by default.

To turn validation on, configure a DefaultServerTransportSecurityValidator with the allowed origins and hosts:

HttpServletStreamableServerTransportProvider transportProvider =
    HttpServletStreamableServerTransportProvider.builder()
        .mcpEndpoint("/mcp")
        .httpHeaderValidator(DefaultServerTransportSecurityValidator.builder()
            .allowedOrigin("http://localhost:*")
            .allowedHost("localhost:*")
            .build())
        .build();

The same httpHeaderValidator(...) method is available on the Stateless and SSE transport builders.

docs.title: Server Capabilities
docs.text:
The server can be configured with various capabilities:

var capabilities = ServerCapabilities.builder()
    .resources(true, true)   // Resource support: subscribe=true, listChanged=true
    .tools(true)             // Tool support with list changes notifications
    .prompts(true)           // Prompt support with list changes notifications
    .completions()           // Enable completions support
    .logging()               // Enable logging support
    .build();

docs.title: Tool Specification
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol allows servers to expose tools that can be invoked by language models. The Java SDK allows implementing Tool Specifications with their handler functions. Tools enable AI models to perform calculations, access external APIs, query databases, and manipulate files.

The recommended approach is to use the builder pattern and CallToolRequest as the handler parameter:

SyncAsync 
// Sync tool specification using builder
var syncToolSpecification = SyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("calculator", schema)
        .description("Basic calculator")
        .build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) -> {
        // Access arguments via request.arguments()
        String operation = (String) request.arguments().get("operation");
        int a = (int) request.arguments().get("a");
        int b = (int) request.arguments().get("b");
        // Tool implementation
        return CallToolResult.builder()
            .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Result: " + result)))
            .build();
    })
    .build();

// Async tool specification using builder
var asyncToolSpecification = AsyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("calculator", schema)
        .description("Basic calculator")
        .build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) -> {
        // Access arguments via request.arguments()
        String operation = (String) request.arguments().get("operation");
        int a = (int) request.arguments().get("a");
        int b = (int) request.arguments().get("b");
        // Tool implementation
        return Mono.just(CallToolResult.builder()
            .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Result: " + result)))
            .build());
    })
    .build();

The Tool specification includes a Tool definition with name, description, and inputSchema followed by a call handler that implements the tool's logic. The handler receives McpSyncServerExchange/McpAsyncServerExchange for client interaction and a CallToolRequest containing the tool arguments.

You can also register tools directly on the server builder using the toolCall convenience method:

var server = McpServer.sync(transportProvider)
    .toolCall(
        Tool.builder("echo", schema).description("Echoes input").build(),
        (exchange, request) -> CallToolResult.builder()
            .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent(request.arguments().get("text").toString())))
            .build()
    )
    .build();

docs.title: Tool Input Validation
docs.text:
By default the server validates incoming tool arguments against the tool's inputSchema before invoking the handler. When validation fails, the call returns a CallToolResult with isError set and a textual error, rather than reaching your handler. Validation uses the configured JsonSchemaValidator (or the default from McpJsonDefaults.getSchemaValidator()), and can be turned off on the server builder:

var server = McpServer.sync(transportProvider)
    .validateToolInputs(false)   // default is true
    .build();

The embedded JSON Schema documents themselves (Tool.inputSchema, Tool.outputSchema, and elicitation requestedSchema) are validated against the JSON Schema 2020-12 meta-schema (SEP-1613). Malformed schemas are rejected at build time (McpServer.build()) and when calling addTool(), throwing an IllegalArgumentException that names the offending field. A schema that declares a different dialect via $schema is accepted without meta-schema validation.

docs.title: Tool Result Content Types
docs.text:
Besides TextContent, a CallToolResult can return images, audio, and embedded resources — any combination of these can appear in the same result's content list:

var syncToolSpecification = SyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("generate-report", schema)
        .description("Generates a report with mixed content")
        .build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) -> {
        var text = TextContent.builder("Report summary:").build();

        // Image content: base64-encoded data + MIME type
        var image = ImageContent.builder(base64PngData, "image/png").build();

        // Audio content: base64-encoded data + MIME type
        var audio = AudioContent.builder(base64WavData, "audio/wav").build();

        // Embedded resource: wraps a TextResourceContents or BlobResourceContents
        var resourceContents = TextResourceContents.builder("report://details", "Full details...")
            .mimeType("text/plain")
            .build();
        var embeddedResource = EmbeddedResource.builder(resourceContents).build();

        return CallToolResult.builder()
            .content(List.of(text, image, audio, embeddedResource))
            .isError(false)
            .build();
    })
    .build();

ImageContent.builder(data, mimeType) and AudioContent.builder(data, mimeType) both take base64-encoded binary data. EmbeddedResource.builder(resourceContents) wraps either a TextResourceContents (for text data) or a BlobResourceContents (for base64-encoded binary data) — see Reading Binary Resources for the BlobResourceContents shape.

docs.title: Filtering the Tool Listing per Request
docs.text:
By default every registered tool is advertised to every caller. Over an HTTP transport you can vary the tools/list response per request — to hide tools the caller is not authorized to see, or to trim a large catalog down to a relevant subset — by registering one or more tool filters.

The filter receives the McpTransportContext extracted from the current request, so it can key on HTTP headers, a token, a resolved principal, or anything else your contextExtractor puts there.

SyncAsync 
McpServer.sync(transportProvider)
    .tools(publicTool, adminTool)
    .addToolFilter((transportContext, tool) ->
        !tool.name().startsWith("admin-") || isAdmin(transportContext))
    .build();

McpServer.async(transportProvider)
    .tools(publicTool, adminTool)
    .addToolFilter((transportContext, tool) -> {
        if (!tool.name().startsWith("admin-")) {
            return Mono.just(true);
        }
        return isAdmin(transportContext); // Mono<Boolean>
    })
    .build();

The same addToolFilter(...) method is available on the stateless builders.

Hiding a tool does not make it unreachable

The filter controls advertisement only. A hidden tool called by name still executes: you MUST enforce permissions in the tool's call handler. Use the filter to control what a caller is told about, not what they are allowed to do.

Evaluation semantics

  • The filter is consulted on every listing request and never cached, so the same session may legitimately see different results for two successive requests carrying different credentials.
  • Registration order is preserved; only omissions happen.
  • Returning Mono.empty() from an async filter omits the tool. An error fails the whole listing request rather than silently hiding tools: a client cannot tell a filtered-down listing from a partial one, and MCP has no way to signal "this listing was incomplete, retry".
  • A filter that errors is logged server-side and reported to the client as an opaque -32603 Internal error with no data. If you want the client to see a specific error, throw an McpError, those are passed through.
  • Filters accumulate as a boolean AND: a tool is listed only when every registered filter accepts it, so a later addToolFilter(...) can never widen access. Evaluation follows registration order and short-circuits on the first filter that hides a tool.

  • toolFilters(Consumer<List<...>>) hands you the list of filters registered so far, so you can inspect, reorder or clear them before building — useful when filters come from several places:

    McpServer.sync(transportProvider)
    .addToolFilter(tenantFilter)
    .toolFilters(filters -> filters.add(0, cheapDenyAllForAnonymousFilter))
    .build();

  • Tools are tested one at a time, so a filter that performs I/O per tool costs one round trip per tool. Sync filters also run on a shared scheduler thread — not the request thread — unless immediateExecution(true) is set, so thread-bound request state (Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder, MDC, custom ThreadLocal holders) is not visible inside the filter. For both reasons, resolve per-request state once in the transport's contextExtractor, which does run on the request thread, and read only the extracted context in the filter:

    // transport builder: one authorization lookup, on the request thread,
// shared by every tool tested in this request
var transportProvider = HttpServletStreamableServerTransportProvider.builder()
    .contextExtractor(request -> McpTransportContext.create(
            Map.of("perms", introspect(request.getHeader("Authorization")))))
    // ...
    .build();

// server builder: the filter reads only the extracted context
McpServer.sync(transportProvider)
    .addToolFilter((context, tool) ->
            ((Set<String>) context.get("perms")).contains(tool.name()))
    .build();

  • notifications/tools/list_changed is not filtered. It is a server-initiated broadcast with no request in flight, so there is no context to evaluate. A client may be told something changed when its own visible set did not; it gets the correct view on its next tools/list. Consider disabling this notification entirely when using tool filters.

  • With STDIO there is no per-request metadata, so the filter receives McpTransportContext.EMPTY and has nothing to key on.

docs.title: Resource Specification
docs.text:
Specification of a resource with its handler function. Resources provide context to AI models by exposing data such as: File contents, Database records, API responses, System information, Application state.

SyncAsync 
// Sync resource specification
var syncResourceSpecification = new McpServerFeatures.SyncResourceSpecification(
    Resource.builder("custom://resource", "name")
        .description("description")
        .mimeType("text/plain")
        .build(),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        // Resource read implementation
        return ReadResourceResult.builder(contents).build();
    }
);

// Async resource specification
var asyncResourceSpecification = new McpServerFeatures.AsyncResourceSpecification(
    Resource.builder("custom://resource", "name")
        .description("description")
        .mimeType("text/plain")
        .build(),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        // Resource read implementation
        return Mono.just(ReadResourceResult.builder(contents).build());
    }
);

docs.title: Reading Binary Resources
docs.text:
Binary resources (images, PDFs, audio, etc.) are returned as BlobResourceContents, which carries base64-encoded data instead of the plain text field used by TextResourceContents:

var binaryResourceSpecification = new McpServerFeatures.SyncResourceSpecification(
    Resource.builder("file:///logo.png", "Logo")
        .description("Application logo")
        .mimeType("image/png")
        .build(),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        String base64Data = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(readLogoBytes());
        return ReadResourceResult.builder(List.of(
                BlobResourceContents.builder(request.uri(), base64Data)
                    .mimeType("image/png")
                    .build()))
            .build();
    }
);

ReadResourceResult accepts a list mixing TextResourceContents and BlobResourceContents, so a single resource read can return multiple representations if needed.

docs.title: Resource Subscriptions
docs.text:
When the subscribe capability is enabled, clients can subscribe to specific resources and receive targeted notifications/resources/updated notifications when those resources change. Only sessions that have explicitly subscribed to a given URI receive the notification — not every connected client.

Enable subscription support in the server capabilities:

McpSyncServer server = McpServer.sync(transportProvider)
    .serverInfo("my-server", "1.0.0")
    .capabilities(ServerCapabilities.builder()
        .resources(true, false)  // subscribe=true, listChanged=false
        .build())
    .resources(myResourceSpec)
    .build();

When a subscribed resource changes, notify only the interested sessions:

SyncAsync 
server.notifyResourcesUpdated(
    new McpSchema.ResourcesUpdatedNotification("custom://resource")
);

server.notifyResourcesUpdated(
    new McpSchema.ResourcesUpdatedNotification("custom://resource")
).subscribe();

If no sessions are subscribed to the given URI the call completes immediately without sending any messages. Subscription state is automatically cleaned up when a client session closes.

docs.title: Resource Template Specification
docs.text:
Resource templates allow servers to expose parameterized resources using URI templates:

// Resource template specification
var resourceTemplateSpec = new McpServerFeatures.SyncResourceTemplateSpecification(
    ResourceTemplate.builder("file://{path}", "File Resource")
        .description("Access files by path")
        .mimeType("application/octet-stream")
        .build(),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        // Read the file at the requested URI
        return ReadResourceResult.builder(contents).build();
    }
);

docs.title: Prompt Specification
docs.text:
As part of the Prompting capabilities, MCP provides a standardized way for servers to expose prompt templates to clients. The Prompt Specification is a structured template for AI model interactions that enables consistent message formatting, parameter substitution, context injection, response formatting, and instruction templating.

SyncAsync 
// Sync prompt specification
var syncPromptSpecification = new McpServerFeatures.SyncPromptSpecification(
    Prompt.builder("greeting")
        .description("description")
        .arguments(List.of(
            PromptArgument.builder("name")
                .description("description")
                .required(true)
                .build()
        ))
        .build(),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        // Prompt implementation
        return GetPromptResult.builder(messages).description(description).build();
    }
);

// Async prompt specification
var asyncPromptSpecification = new McpServerFeatures.AsyncPromptSpecification(
    Prompt.builder("greeting")
        .description("description")
        .arguments(List.of(
            PromptArgument.builder("name")
                .description("description")
                .required(true)
                .build()
        ))
        .build(),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        // Prompt implementation
        return Mono.just(GetPromptResult.builder(messages).description(description).build());
    }
);

The prompt definition includes name (identifier for the prompt), description (purpose of the prompt), and list of arguments (parameters for templating). The handler function processes requests and returns formatted templates. The first argument is McpSyncServerExchange/McpAsyncServerExchange for client interaction, and the second argument is a GetPromptRequest instance.

docs.title: Prompts with Embedded Resources and Images
docs.text:
A prompt's messages can carry EmbeddedResource or ImageContent instead of plain text by passing them as the content argument of PromptMessage.builder(role, content):

// Prompt that embeds a resource's content in one of its messages
var promptWithResource = new McpServerFeatures.SyncPromptSpecification(
    Prompt.builder("review-file")
        .description("Reviews a file, embedding its content in the prompt")
        .arguments(List.of(PromptArgument.builder("resourceUri").required(true).build()))
        .build(),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        String resourceUri = (String) request.arguments().get("resourceUri");
        var resourceContents = TextResourceContents.builder(resourceUri, loadFileContent(resourceUri))
            .mimeType("text/plain")
            .build();
        var embeddedResource = EmbeddedResource.builder(resourceContents).build();

        return GetPromptResult.builder(List.of(
                PromptMessage.builder(Role.USER, embeddedResource).build(),
                PromptMessage.builder(Role.USER, TextContent.builder("Please review the file above.").build()).build()))
            .build();
    }
);

// Prompt that embeds an image in one of its messages
var promptWithImage = new McpServerFeatures.SyncPromptSpecification(
    Prompt.builder("describe-image")
        .description("Asks the model to describe an embedded image")
        .arguments(List.of())
        .build(),
    (exchange, request) -> GetPromptResult.builder(List.of(
            PromptMessage.builder(Role.USER, ImageContent.builder(base64PngData, "image/png").build()).build(),
            PromptMessage.builder(Role.USER, TextContent.builder("Describe the image above.").build()).build()))
        .build()
);

docs.title: Completion Specification
docs.text:
Completions allow servers to provide argument autocompletion suggestions for prompts and resources:

SyncAsync 
// Sync completion specification
var syncCompletionSpec = new McpServerFeatures.SyncCompletionSpecification(
    new McpSchema.PromptReference("greeting"),  // Reference to a prompt
    (exchange, request) -> {
        String argName = request.argument().name();
        String partial = request.argument().value();
        // Return matching suggestions
        List<String> suggestions = findMatches(partial);
        return new McpSchema.CompleteResult(
            new McpSchema.CompleteResult.CompleteCompletion(suggestions, suggestions.size(), false)
        );
    }
);

// Async completion specification
var asyncCompletionSpec = new McpServerFeatures.AsyncCompletionSpecification(
    new McpSchema.PromptReference("greeting"),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        String argName = request.argument().name();
        String partial = request.argument().value();
        List<String> suggestions = findMatches(partial);
        return Mono.just(new McpSchema.CompleteResult(
            new McpSchema.CompleteResult.CompleteCompletion(suggestions, suggestions.size(), false)
        ));
    }
);

Completions can be registered for both PromptReference and ResourceReference types. A ResourceReference completion suggests values for a resource template's URI parameters instead of a prompt's arguments:

SyncAsync 
// Sync completion specification for a resource template argument
var syncResourceCompletionSpec = new McpServerFeatures.SyncCompletionSpecification(
    new McpSchema.ResourceReference("file://{path}"),  // Reference to a resource template
    (exchange, request) -> {
        String argName = request.argument().name();
        String partial = request.argument().value();
        // Return matching suggestions, e.g. matching file paths
        List<String> suggestions = findMatchingPaths(partial);
        return new McpSchema.CompleteResult(
            new McpSchema.CompleteResult.CompleteCompletion(suggestions, suggestions.size(), false)
        );
    }
);

// Async completion specification for a resource template argument
var asyncResourceCompletionSpec = new McpServerFeatures.AsyncCompletionSpecification(
    new McpSchema.ResourceReference("file://{path}"),
    (exchange, request) -> {
        String argName = request.argument().name();
        String partial = request.argument().value();
        List<String> suggestions = findMatchingPaths(partial);
        return Mono.just(new McpSchema.CompleteResult(
            new McpSchema.CompleteResult.CompleteCompletion(suggestions, suggestions.size(), false)
        ));
    }
);

docs.title: Using Sampling from a Server
docs.text:
To use Sampling capabilities, connect to a client that supports sampling. No special server configuration is needed, but verify client sampling support before making requests. Learn about client sampling support.

Once connected to a compatible client, the server can request language model generations:

Sync APIAsync API 
// Create a server
McpSyncServer server = McpServer.sync(transportProvider)
    .serverInfo("my-server", "1.0.0")
    .build();

// Define a tool that uses sampling
var calculatorTool = SyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("ai-calculator", schema)
        .description("Performs calculations using AI")
        .build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) -> {
        // Check if client supports sampling
        if (exchange.getClientCapabilities().sampling() == null) {
            return CallToolResult.builder()
                .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Client does not support AI capabilities")))
                .build();
        }

        // Create a sampling request
        CreateMessageRequest samplingRequest = CreateMessageRequest.builder(
                List.of(new McpSchema.SamplingMessage(McpSchema.Role.USER,
                    new McpSchema.TextContent("Calculate: " + request.arguments().get("expression")))),
                100)
            .modelPreferences(McpSchema.ModelPreferences.builder()
                .hints(List.of(
                    McpSchema.ModelHint.of("claude-3-sonnet"),
                    McpSchema.ModelHint.of("claude")
                ))
                .intelligencePriority(0.8)
                .speedPriority(0.5)
                .build())
            .systemPrompt("You are a helpful calculator assistant. Provide only the numerical answer.")
            .build();

        // Request sampling from the client
        CreateMessageResult result = exchange.createMessage(samplingRequest);

        // Process the result
        String answer = ((McpSchema.TextContent) result.content()).text();
        return CallToolResult.builder()
            .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent(answer)))
            .build();
    })
    .build();

// Add the tool to the server
server.addTool(calculatorTool);

// Create a server
McpAsyncServer server = McpServer.async(transportProvider)
    .serverInfo("my-server", "1.0.0")
    .build();

// Define a tool that uses sampling
var calculatorTool = AsyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("ai-calculator", schema)
        .description("Performs calculations using AI")
        .build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) -> {
        // Check if client supports sampling
        if (exchange.getClientCapabilities().sampling() == null) {
            return Mono.just(CallToolResult.builder()
                .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Client does not support AI capabilities")))
                .build());
        }

        // Create a sampling request
        CreateMessageRequest samplingRequest = CreateMessageRequest.builder(
                List.of(new McpSchema.SamplingMessage(McpSchema.Role.USER,
                    new McpSchema.TextContent("Calculate: " + request.arguments().get("expression")))),
                100)
            .modelPreferences(McpSchema.ModelPreferences.builder()
                .hints(List.of(
                    McpSchema.ModelHint.of("claude-3-sonnet"),
                    McpSchema.ModelHint.of("claude")
                ))
                .intelligencePriority(0.8)
                .speedPriority(0.5)
                .build())
            .systemPrompt("You are a helpful calculator assistant. Provide only the numerical answer.")
            .build();

        // Request sampling from the client
        return exchange.createMessage(samplingRequest)
            .map(result -> {
                String answer = ((McpSchema.TextContent) result.content()).text();
                return CallToolResult.builder()
                    .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent(answer)))
                    .build();
            });
    })
    .build();

// Add the tool to the server
server.addTool(calculatorTool)
    .subscribe();

The CreateMessageRequest object allows you to specify: Content - the input text or image for the model, Model Preferences - hints and priorities for model selection, System Prompt - instructions for the model's behavior and Max Tokens - maximum length of the generated response.

docs.title: Using Elicitation from a Server
docs.text:
Servers can request user input from connected clients that support elicitation:

var tool = SyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("confirm-action", schema)
        .description("Confirms an action with the user")
        .build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) -> {
        // Check if client supports elicitation
        if (exchange.getClientCapabilities().elicitation() == null) {
            return CallToolResult.builder()
                .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Client does not support elicitation")))
                .build();
        }

        // Request user confirmation
        ElicitRequest elicitRequest = ElicitFormRequest.builder("Do you want to proceed with this action?", Map.of(
                "type", "object",
                "properties", Map.of("confirmed", Map.of("type", "boolean"))
            ))
            .build();

        ElicitResult result = exchange.elicit(elicitRequest);

        if (result.action() == ElicitResult.Action.ACCEPT) {
            // User accepted
            return CallToolResult.builder()
                .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Action confirmed")))
                .build();
        } else {
            return CallToolResult.builder()
                .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Action declined")))
                .build();
        }
    })
    .build();

To request out-of-band URL elicitation, such as a user authorizing an OAuth flow:

var urlTool = SyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("oauth-auth", schema)
        .description("Authenticates via OAuth")
        .build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) -> {
        // Request URL elicitation from client
        if (
                exchange.getClientCapabilities().elicitation() != null 
                && exchange.getClientCapabilities().elicitation().url() != null
        ) {
            ElicitRequest urlRequest = McpSchema.ElicitUrlRequest
                    .builder("Please authenticate", "https://example.com/oauth", "oauth-123").build();
            ElicitResult result = exchange.elicit(urlRequest);
            // handle result.action == CANCELLED or DENIED
            if (result.action() != ElicitResult.Action.ACCEPT) {
                return CallToolResult.builder()
                        .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Authentication failed or cancelled")))
                        .build();
            }
        }

        // wait for user to visit the URL
        return CallToolResult.builder()
                .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Authentication successful")))
                .build();
    })
    .build();

docs.title: Elicitation with Enum Values (SEP-1330)
docs.text:
For form elicitation, the SDK provides typed helpers to build requestedSchema properties that render as single-select or multi-select choices, with or without human-readable titles:

// Untitled single-select: plain enum values, no separate display titles
var untitledSingle = UntitledSingleSelectEnumSchema.builder()
    .enumValues("small", "medium", "large")
    .build();

// Titled single-select: value/title pairs via oneOf+const
var titledSingle = TitledSingleSelectEnumSchema.builder()
    .oneOf(new EnumSchemaOption("sm", "Small"),
           new EnumSchemaOption("md", "Medium"),
           new EnumSchemaOption("lg", "Large"))
    .build();

// Untitled multi-select: an array property whose items are an enum
var untitledMulti = UntitledMultiSelectEnumSchema
    .builder(UntitledMultiSelectItems.builder().enumValues("red", "green", "blue").build())
    .build();

// Titled multi-select: array items with value/title pairs via anyOf+const
var titledMulti = TitledMultiSelectEnumSchema
    .builder(TitledMultiSelectItems.builder()
        .anyOf(new EnumSchemaOption("red", "Red"), new EnumSchemaOption("green", "Green"))
        .build())
    .build();

// Convert the typed schema helpers into the plain Map<String, Object> shape
// expected by ElicitRequest.builder(message, requestedSchema)
var mapper = McpJsonDefaults.getMapper();
TypeRef<Map<String, Object>> mapType = new TypeRef<>() {};
Map<String, Object> requestedSchema = Map.of("type", "object", "properties",
        Map.of("size", mapper.convertValue(titledSingle, mapType),
               "colors", mapper.convertValue(titledMulti, mapType)),
        "required", List.of("size", "colors"));

ElicitRequest elicitRequest = ElicitRequest.builder("Choose your options", requestedSchema).build();
ElicitResult result = exchange.createElicitation(elicitRequest);

LegacyTitledEnumSchema (a value list plus a parallel enumNames list, built with .enumValues(...) and .enumNames(...)) is also available for clients that predate SEP-1330's oneOf/anyOf convention, but new schemas should prefer TitledSingleSelectEnumSchema / TitledMultiSelectEnumSchema.

docs.title: Pinging the Client
docs.text:
A server can check that a connected client is still responsive by sending a ping request through the exchange:

var tool = SyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("health-check", emptyJsonSchema).description("Verifies the client is reachable").build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) -> {
        exchange.ping(); // blocks until the client responds, or the request times out
        return CallToolResult.builder()
            .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Client is responsive")))
            .build();
    })
    .build();

The async equivalent, McpAsyncServerExchange.ping(), returns a Mono<Object> that completes when the client responds. Ping requests are subject to the same requestTimeout configured on the server builder.

docs.title: Logging Support
docs.text:
The server provides structured logging capabilities that allow sending log messages to clients with different severity levels. Log notifications can only be sent from within an existing client session, such as tools, resources, and prompts calls.

The server can send log messages using the McpAsyncServerExchange/McpSyncServerExchange object in the tool/resource/prompt handler function:

var tool = AsyncToolSpecification.builder()
    .tool(Tool.builder("logging-test", emptyJsonSchema).description("Test logging notifications").build())
    .callHandler((exchange, request) ->
        exchange.loggingNotification( // Use the exchange to send log messages
            McpSchema.LoggingMessageNotification.builder(McpSchema.LoggingLevel.DEBUG, "Debug message")
              .logger("test-logger")
              .build())
          .then(Mono.just(CallToolResult.builder()
              .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Logging test completed")))
              .build())))
    .build();

var mcpServer = McpServer.async(mcpServerTransportProvider)
  .serverInfo("test-server", "1.0.0")
  .capabilities(
    ServerCapabilities.builder()
      .logging() // Enable logging support
      .tools(true)
      .build())
  .tools(tool)
  .build();

On the client side, you can register a logging consumer to receive log messages from the server:

var mcpClient = McpClient.sync(transport)
        .loggingConsumer(notification -> {
            System.out.println("Received log message: " + notification.data());
        })
        .build();

mcpClient.initialize();
mcpClient.setLoggingLevel(McpSchema.LoggingLevel.INFO);

Clients can control the minimum logging level they receive through the mcpClient.setLoggingLevel(level) request. Messages below the set level will be filtered out. Supported logging levels (in order of increasing severity): DEBUG (0), INFO (1), NOTICE (2), WARNING (3), ERROR (4), CRITICAL (5), ALERT (6), EMERGENCY (7)

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: The SDK provides comprehensive error handling through the McpError class, covering protocol compatibility, transport communication, JSON-RPC messaging, tool execution, resource management, prompt handling, timeouts, and connection issues. This unified error handling approach ensures consistent and reliable error management across both synchronous and asynchronous operations.

docs.title: Two Tiers of Errors
docs.text:
MCP distinguishes between two categories of errors in tool execution:

1. Tool-Level Errors (Recoverable by the LLM)

Use CallToolResult with isError(true) for validation failures, missing arguments, or domain errors the LLM can act on and retry.

// Example: Domain validation failure (e.g., invalid email format)
if (!emailAddress.matches("^[A-Za-z0-9+_.-]+@(.+)$")) {
        return CallToolResult.builder()
        .content(List.of(new McpSchema.TextContent("Invalid argument: 'email' must be a valid email address.")))
        .isError(true)
        .build();
}

The LLM receives this as part of the normal tool response and can self-correct in a subsequent interaction.

2. Protocol-Level Errors (Unrecoverable)

Uncaught exceptions from a tool handler are mapped to a JSON-RPC error response. Use this only for truly unexpected failures (e.g., infrastructure errors such as DB timeout), not for input validation.

// This propagates as a JSON-RPC error — use sparingly
throw new McpError(McpSchema.ErrorCodes.INTERNAL_ERROR, "Unexpected failure");

docs.text: Situation Approach Domain validation failure CallToolResult with isError=true Infrastructure / unexpected error Throw McpError or let it propagate Partial success with a warning CallToolResult with warning in text

docs.title: Java Leads MCP Server Performance Benchmarks with Sub-Millisecond Latency
docs.text: A comprehensive independent benchmark of MCP server implementations across four major languages puts Java at the top of the performance charts — delivering sub-millisecond latency, the highest throughput, and the best CPU efficiency of all tested platforms.

docs.title: The Benchmark
docs.text:
TM Dev Lab published a rigorous performance comparison of MCP server implementations spanning 3.9 million total requests across three independent test rounds. The benchmark evaluated four implementations under identical conditions:

  • Java — Spring Boot 4.0.0 + Spring AI 2.0.0-M2 on Java 21
  • Go — Official MCP SDK v1.2.0
  • Node.js — @modelcontextprotocol/sdk v1.26.0
  • Python — FastMCP 2.12.0+ with FastAPI 0.109.0+

Each server was tested with 50 concurrent virtual users over 5-minute sustained runs in Docker containers (1-core CPU, 1GB memory) on Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS. Four standardized benchmark tools measured CPU-intensive, I/O-intensive, data transformation, and latency-handling scenarios — all with a 0% error rate across every implementation.

docs.text:
The results speak for themselves:

Java achieved the lowest average latency at 0.835 ms — edging out Go's 0.855 ms — while matching its throughput at 1,624 requests per second. Where Java truly stands out is CPU efficiency: at 57.2 RPS per CPU%, it extracts more performance per compute cycle than any other implementation, including Go (50.4).

In CPU-bound workloads like Fibonacci calculation, Java excelled with a 0.369 ms response time, showcasing the JVM's highly optimized just-in-time compilation.

docs.title: A Clear Performance Tier
docs.text:
The benchmark reveals two distinct performance tiers:

  • High-performance tier: Java and Go deliver sub-millisecond latencies and 1,600+ RPS
  • Standard tier: Node.js (12x slower) and Python (31x slower) trail significantly

Java's throughput is 2.9x higher than Node.js and 5.6x higher than Python. For latency-sensitive MCP deployments, the difference is even more pronounced — Java responds 12.8x faster than Node.js and 31.7x faster than Python.

docs.title: What This Means for MCP Developers
docs.text:
For teams building production MCP servers that need to handle high concurrency and low-latency tool interactions, Java with Spring Boot and Spring AI provides a battle-tested, high-performance foundation. The JVM's mature ecosystem, strong typing, and proven scalability make it an excellent choice for enterprise MCP deployments where performance and reliability are paramount.

The full benchmark details, methodology, and raw data are available at TM Dev Lab.
